title: Designing a sales rank by category

facts.text: The service calculates the past week's most popular products by category and lets users view them, with high availability. The general e-commerce site and anything beyond the sales rank calculation are out of scope.

Assumptions: traffic is uneven; an item can be in multiple categories but cannot change category; there are no subcategories; results must be updated hourly, and more popular products might need more frequent updates.
The scale is 10 million products, 1 billion transactions per month and 100 billion read requests per month, a 100:1 read to write ratio.
A transaction is about 40 bytes: created_at 5, product_id 8, category_id 4, seller_id 8, buyer_id 8, quantity 4 and total_price 5 bytes.
That is 40 GB of new transaction content per month (40 bytes times 1 billion transactions) and 1.44 TB in 3 years, assuming most are new transactions rather than updates.
The average load is 400 transactions per second and 40,000 read requests per second.
Raw Sales API server log files go to a managed object store such as Amazon S3, rather than a self-managed distributed file system.
The Sales Rank Service runs MapReduce with the Sales API server logs as input, writing results to an aggregate table sales_rank in a SQL database.
It uses a multi-step MapReduce: first transform records to (category, product_id) with sum(quantity), then perform a distributed sort. The sorted list is inserted into the sales_rank table.
The sales_rank table is indexed on id, category_id and product_id, for log-time lookups instead of scanning the whole table and to keep the data in memory.
To view rankings, the client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Read API server; that server reads the SQL sales_rank table. The public API is REST, with RPC for internal calls.
The 40,000 average read requests per second (higher at peak) should be handled by a memory cache instead of the database, which also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes.
With such a large volume of reads, SQL read replicas might not handle the cache misses, so additional SQL scaling patterns are probably needed.

400 average writes per second (higher at peak) might be tough for a single SQL write master-slave. SQL scaling patterns include federation, denormalization and SQL tuning; some data might also move to NoSQL.

The analytics database could be a data warehouse such as Redshift or BigQuery. Keep a limited time period in the database and the rest in a warehouse or an object store, which handles 40 GB of new content per month.

notes: Chapter has a single source page (the primer solution); no separate concept pages were crawled.
